content: Hives, also known as urticaria, are raised, red, and often itchy welts that appear on the surface of the skin. These welts can vary in size and shape and are typically the result of an allergic reaction to certain substances, such as food or medication. Symptoms of Hives: Hives are characterized by intense itching and swelling of the skin, which manifests as red or skin-colored welts (referred to as wheals) with clearly defined edges. These welts may enlarge, spread, and merge to form larger areas of raised skin. They can also change shape, disappear, and reappear within minutes or hours. A hallmark feature of hives is that they come and go. When pressure is applied to the center of a hive, it turns white, a phenomenon known as blanching. Causes of Hives: Hives occur when the body releases histamine and other chemicals into the bloodstream in response to an allergic reaction. This release leads to itching, swelling, and other symptoms. Common triggers include: Animal dander, particularly from cats. Insect bites or stings. Certain medications. Pollen. Foods such as shellfish, fish, nuts, eggs, and milk. Hives can also result from non-allergic causes, such as: Emotional stress. Extreme cold or sun exposure. Excessive sweating. Underlying illnesses, including lupus, autoimmune diseases, and leukemia. Infections, such as mononucleosis. When swelling occurs around the face, especially the lips and eyes, it is referred to as angioedema. Angioedema can also affect the hands, feet, and throat. Diagnosis: A physician can diagnose hives by examining the skin. If there is a history of allergies, the diagnosis becomes more straightforward. In some cases, skin or blood tests may be performed to confirm an allergic reaction and identify the specific trigger. A skin biopsy may be conducted to confirm the diagnosis in uncertain cases. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: Immediate medical attention is required if you experience: Fainting. Shortness of breath. Tightness in the throat. Swelling of the tongue or face. Wheezing. Contact your healthcare provider if the hives are severe, cause significant discomfort, or do not respond to self-care measures. Treatment Options: Mild cases of hives may not require treatment, as they often resolve on their own. To alleviate itching and swelling: Avoid hot baths or showers. Refrain from wearing tight-fitting clothing that may irritate the affected area. Take antihistamines, such as diphenhydramine (which may cause drowsiness), loratadine, or cetirizine. Severe reactions, particularly those involving throat swelling, may necessitate emergency treatment with an epinephrine (adrenaline) injection or corticosteroids. Hives in the throat can obstruct the airway, making breathing difficult. Prognosis: While hives can be uncomfortable, they are generally harmless and tend to resolve on their own. In many cases, the exact cause of hives cannot be determined. Possible Complications: Anaphylaxis, a life-threatening allergic reaction that can cause difficulty breathing. Swelling in the throat, which can lead to a potentially fatal airway obstruction. Prevention: Avoid exposure to substances that trigger allergic reactions. After an episode of hives, avoid wearing tight-fitting clothing and taking hot baths or showers, as these can exacerbate symptoms.
